title: But what is the Fourier Transform?  A visual introduction.
beats: Shows the finished animation up front, promises sound first then wider domains
Pure A at 440 Hz as air pressure vs time; D is the same shape with fewer beats
Asks what the graph of two notes played together looks like; sum point by point
Four frequencies yield a messy wave; microphone only sees the sum; unmixing paint
Goal: build a machine that treats one frequency differently; slow 3 Hz signal on 0-4.5 s
Wrap the graph around a circle via a rotating vector whose length is the graph height
Flags two distinct frequencies: signal frequency vs winding frequency, which we can vary
Sweeps winding frequency; pretty shapes, but reminds it is only wrapping
Viewer senses something special at 3 Hz: peaks all right, valleys all left
Treat the wound graph as a metal wire; track its center of mass
New plot: x-coordinate of center of mass vs winding frequency; spike at 3
Sums up three objects: original graph, wound graph, frequency plot
Spike at zero is just the upward shift; chose shifted cosine to avoid negatives
Names it the almost Fourier transform; real one comes later
Repeat with 2 Hz signal: spike at 2
Add 2 Hz and 3 Hz; chaos then alignment at 2 and at 3
Linearity stated; viewer invited to pause and convince themselves
Machine unmixes the paint as promised
Sound editing: smush a high-pitch spike, then inverse transform
Inverse transform is a little bit of a lie, more next video
Center of mass is 2D, so use the complex plane
Euler's formula as walking around a unit circle; e^(2 pi i t), then times f
Negative sign for clockwise; multiply by g(t) to draw the wound graph
Center of mass approx by sampling points and averaging, limit becomes integral
Integral of complex function needs no calculus: it is just center of mass
True transform drops the divide-by-interval; longer persistence scales the peak
Summary: g-hat takes frequency, outputs complex number; notation introduced last
Daunting formula decoded part by part
Infinite bounds as limit of finite intervals

theory: The video builds a physical machine (wrap, then center of mass) and only after the machine has been run on three examples does it translate each part into symbols. Notation arrives as a compression of an already-owned picture, and the final formula is presented as a recap rather than a definition. The named stepping stone (almost Fourier transform) lets the true definition arrive as a one-line diff.
velocity: Orchestrator: allow a provisional 'almost' concept as a first-class playbook node, with refinement steps queued as diffs
Scene builder: keep a persistent 3-panel layout (input, transformed view, readout plot) across examples so only the data changes
Voice: when animation complexity spikes, insert an 'it's still just X' line
Learner model: gate notation until the learner has seen the mechanism produce the key result on 2+ examples
Evals: check that the final formula is narrated part-by-part mapping to prior visuals
quote: convince yourself that what I just said is actually true
